Defining “top” game programmers requires balancing technical innovation, influence on design and business, and enduring cultural impact. The following ten figures are widely regarded as foundational or transformative in game programming from the medium’s inception through the modern era. Each entry explains the programmer’s key contributions and why they matter.

1.   Ralph H. Baer — Architect of the home video-game era

*   Developed the “Brown Box” and licensed it as the Magnavox Odyssey (1972), the first home video-game console.
*   Invented core concepts for consumer game hardware: user controllers, game switching, on-screen scoring.
*   Importance: moved games out of labs and arcades into living rooms; set the hardware + software model for consoles.

1.   Nolan Bushnell — Early commercialization through code and entrepreneurship

*   Wrote early code and co-founded Atari; shepherded Pong (with Allan Alcorn) into a cultural phenomenon.
*   Established the arcade business model and rapid iteration culture in game development.
*   Importance: bridged technical execution and mass-market productization; created an industry ecosystem.

1.   Steve Russell — Creator of Spacewar! and pioneer of interactive real-time games

*   Implemented Spacewar! (1962) on the PDP-1, one of the first interactive, real-time graphical computer games.
*   Demonstrated direct manipulation of graphical output, physics-like motion, and multiplayer interaction.
*   Importance: served as a direct technical and conceptual ancestor to all real-time action games.

1.   Shigeru Miyamoto — Designer-engineer who reshaped game programming goals

*   Not primarily a systems coder but an active programmer-designer at Nintendo whose iterative prototyping drove software architecture for Donkey Kong, Super Mario Bros., and The Legend of Zelda.
*   Pushed gameplay-first engineering: tight control of physics, collision, level scripting, and memory constraints on NES/Famicom.
*   Importance: influenced how programmers structure code around gameplay, prioritizing responsiveness and player experience.

1.   John Carmack — Master of real-time 3D engines

*   Principal programmer behind id Software classics (Wolfenstein 3D, Doom, Quake). Invented techniques: binary space partitioning (BSP) for indoor rendering, efficient software rasterizers, precalculated lightmaps, and early networked multiplayer engines.
*   Open-sourced major engines, accelerating education and engine-based development.
*   Importance: defined 3D shooter architecture, performance-focused coding practices, and id Tech lineage that underpins modern engines.

1.   Will Wright — Simulation systems architect

*   Architect of SimCity and later The Sims; created extensible simulation engines modeling emergent behavior from simple rules and player-directed parameters.
*   Advanced procedural systems, sandbox design, and content pipelines emphasizing authorable, scalable simulation.
*   Importance: showed how programming can create systems that produce rich, unscripted play and long-term engagement.

1.   Yu Suzuki — Technical auteur of arcade hardware and programming innovation

*   Led programming and design at Sega (Hang-On, Out Run, Virtua Fighter); built custom hardware and physics/graphics pipelines for high-performance arcade experiences.
*   Pioneered force-feedback, sprite-scaling techniques, and early 3D arcade rendering.
*   Importance: advanced bespoke hardware-software co-design and immersive realtime systems.

1.   Roberta Williams / Ken Williams team — Early adventure-engine innovation (scripting and parser systems)

*   Ken implemented the engines that powered Sierra’s adventure games; Roberta led design and narrative.
*   Built modular parsers, inventory/state systems, and cinematic scripting for large narrative games (King’s Quest series).
*   Importance: established how game code supports branching narratives, stateful world simulation, and user-language parsing.

1.   Markus Persson (Notch) — Modern indie-engine and distribution disruptor

*   Coded the original Minecraft prototype and its incremental engine, prioritizing buildability, an infinite procedurally generated world, and mod-friendly architecture.
*   Demonstrated how a single programmer's iterative development can create a platform with massive social and creative impact.
*   Importance: popularized voxel-based procedural generation and showed the economic and cultural power of small-team development.

1.   Hideo Kojima (programming influence and systems-minded auteur)

*   While primarily known as designer-director, Kojima’s hands-on approach to scripting, engine decisions, and cinematic tech (Metal Gear series) drove ambitious systems combining stealth AI, scripted events, and complex state machines.
*   Pushed integration of narrative-driven engines, motion capture pipelines, and cinematic tools into mainstream games.
*   Importance: influenced how game programmers integrate narrative, AI, and cinematic systems at high technical ambition.

Notes on selection and omissions

*   This list emphasizes programmers (or programmer-designers) whose code, engines, or system architectures changed how games are made. It includes hardware-software pioneers, engine authors, and influential indie developers.
*   Many other essential figures—Al Alcorn, Gary Gygax’s analog-to-digital lineage, Alexey Pajitnov (Tetris), Sid Meier (programmer-designer; simulation AI), Tim Sweeney (Unreal Engine), Amy Hennig (narrative systems), John Romero (design/programming at id), Brenda Laurel, and numerous unsung engine architects—are also profoundly influential. Different criteria (pure technical breakthroughs, cultural impact, commercial success, or breadth of influence) would yield different top-ten lists.
*   For time-sensitive or more exhaustive rankings, focus areas can be narrowed: engine authors, AI pioneers, graphics programmers, or indie innovators to highlight specialists.

Define "great programmer". If you're thinking of someone who can create an amazing game experience pretty much single-handedly, yes, I'd second Sid Meier, and add Brian Reynolds, who made an amazing Civ 2 prototype when he was working remotely in England (long before the days of distributed workforces); keep in mind, however, that Sid and Brian both self-identify as designers even though they have programming skills.

But for someone who defines "great programmer" as a person who loves solving really tough technical challenges, especially around performance, rendering, and modern consoles, I'd nominate Phil Teschner, and throw in Sam Lantiga at Valve.

If a great programmer is a visionary who helps create new technology that becomes an industry standard, Alex St. John should be on the list for his work on DirectX (which was the foundation for the Xbox).

If a great programmer is able to impart her knowledge to others and make the team better, it's a different list entirely. If a great programmer creates an amazing experience based on the capabilities of the platform, I'm sure there are many people who broke ground in early social and mobile games and created revolutionary experiences. If a great programmer makes an existing engine do things its creators never dreamed of, I'm sure Epic has some suggestions.

Great programmers also have a very different role today in game development than they did 20 years ago. Because game development has changed so much, you can specialize to an incredible degree; specialization in, say, graphics or AI doesn't make you greater (or less great) than your counterparts 20 years ago. Also keep in mind that because the industry is much larger than it was 20 years ago, there are many incredible programmers who don't get the PR love because they're working on a 200- or 300-person team; that doesn't mean they're less talented, just that the industry has changed significantly and programmers are often the unsung heros who help make the vision of the producers and designers a reality.

I think most of the answers here have good nominees, so I won’t repeat the most popular ones (Bill Budge, Ken Silverman, Jon Freeman and Anne Westfall, etc.), but I’d like to nominate a programmer who is often overlooked, but what he achieved was astounding.

This guy developed a game with a complete windowing GUI on an Apple II. It didn’t predate Pinball Construction Set, but what it did was much more complex. Whenever you clicked on a game element (say, a ship engine), a new window would pop up, populated with everything pertinent to that item. You could drag and drop within that window, and then dismiss it when you were done with it. Sound familiar?

And this paradigm worked for the whole game, not just some parts. Where many other games of the era made you type in a command (e.g. Wizardry for spells), this game employed icons.

This game was released about the same time as the first Macintosh, so it’s unlikely that the game tried to “copy” the Mac interface; there simply wasn’t enough time. The programmer said his GUI was inspired directly from the developments at Xerox PARC (the same place Apple took their inspiration for the Mac).

![Image 23](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-1b11349275d8f0ae5533834def0c8fda-lq)

While the gameplay, setting and objectives were engaging, that asn’t the point. This game employed an entire GUI that wouldn’t be commonplace for another 11 years, all in 64K of memory!

And that isn’t all. The game, if left unattended, would execute a self-running demo for the game’s planned sequel!

The programmer was Bruce Webster and the game was SunDog: Frozen Legacy. Why many probably haven’t heard of him is because after this game, he suffered from game programming burn out and quit the industry. He went on to write articles for BYTE magazine and to teach, also becoming CTO of a software company at one point. Now he’s teaching senior-level programming classes at his alma mater, BYU.

Webster developed the Apple II version of the game. About a year later, FTL released an Atari ST version of the game. He said one of his proudest moments was upon meeting one of the developers of the Atari ST version of the game. He said they were able to left entire sections of his code and re-use them verbatim because he used a Berkley-compliant Pascal compiler for the Apple II version, and they used a Berkley-compliant Pascal compiler for the Atari ST version as well. A great deal of the Atari ST version of the game is actually Webster’s code, though he never actively participated in its development.

Had he not suffered burn-out, the world may have been blessed with SunDog II: Old Scores to Settle and SunDog III: Blows Against the Empire. Too bad. If SunDog was anything to judge by, they would have been blasts.

Defining “top” game programmers requires balancing technical innovation, influence on design and business, and enduring cultural impact. The following ten figures are widely regarded as foundational or transformative in game programming from the medium’s inception through the modern era. Each entry explains the programmer’s key contributions and why they matter.

1.   Ralph H. Baer — Architect of the home video-game era

*   Developed the “Brown Box” and licensed it as the Magnavox Odyssey (1972), the first home video-game console.
*   Invented core concepts for consumer game hardware: user controllers, game switching, on-screen scoring.
*   Importance: moved games out of labs and arcades into living rooms; set the hardware + software model for consoles.

1.   Nolan Bushnell — Early commercialization through code and entrepreneurship

*   Wrote early code and co-founded Atari; shepherded Pong (with Allan Alcorn) into a cultural phenomenon.
*   Established the arcade business model and rapid iteration culture in game development.
*   Importance: bridged technical execution and mass-market productization; created an industry ecosystem.

1.   Steve Russell — Creator of Spacewar! and pioneer of interactive real-time games

*   Implemented Spacewar! (1962) on the PDP-1, one of the first interactive, real-time graphical computer games.
*   Demonstrated direct manipulation of graphical output, physics-like motion, and multiplayer interaction.
*   Importance: served as a direct technical and conceptual ancestor to all real-time action games.

1.   Shigeru Miyamoto — Designer-engineer who reshaped game programming goals

*   Not primarily a systems coder but an active programmer-designer at Nintendo whose iterative prototyping drove software architecture for Donkey Kong, Super Mario Bros., and The Legend of Zelda.
*   Pushed gameplay-first engineering: tight control of physics, collision, level scripting, and memory constraints on NES/Famicom.
*   Importance: influenced how programmers structure code around gameplay, prioritizing responsiveness and player experience.

1.   John Carmack — Master of real-time 3D engines

*   Principal programmer behind id Software classics (Wolfenstein 3D, Doom, Quake). Invented techniques: binary space partitioning (BSP) for indoor rendering, efficient software rasterizers, precalculated lightmaps, and early networked multiplayer engines.
*   Open-sourced major engines, accelerating education and engine-based development.
*   Importance: defined 3D shooter architecture, performance-focused coding practices, and id Tech lineage that underpins modern engines.

1.   Will Wright — Simulation systems architect

*   Architect of SimCity and later The Sims; created extensible simulation engines modeling emergent behavior from simple rules and player-directed parameters.
*   Advanced procedural systems, sandbox design, and content pipelines emphasizing authorable, scalable simulation.
*   Importance: showed how programming can create systems that produce rich, unscripted play and long-term engagement.

1.   Yu Suzuki — Technical auteur of arcade hardware and programming innovation

*   Led programming and design at Sega (Hang-On, Out Run, Virtua Fighter); built custom hardware and physics/graphics pipelines for high-performance arcade experiences.
*   Pioneered force-feedback, sprite-scaling techniques, and early 3D arcade rendering.
*   Importance: advanced bespoke hardware-software co-design and immersive realtime systems.

1.   Roberta Williams / Ken Williams team — Early adventure-engine innovation (scripting and parser systems)

*   Ken implemented the engines that powered Sierra’s adventure games; Roberta led design and narrative.
*   Built modular parsers, inventory/state systems, and cinematic scripting for large narrative games (King’s Quest series).
*   Importance: established how game code supports branching narratives, stateful world simulation, and user-language parsing.

1.   Markus Persson (Notch) — Modern indie-engine and distribution disruptor

*   Coded the original Minecraft prototype and its incremental engine, prioritizing buildability, an infinite procedurally generated world, and mod-friendly architecture.
*   Demonstrated how a single programmer's iterative development can create a platform with massive social and creative impact.
*   Importance: popularized voxel-based procedural generation and showed the economic and cultural power of small-team development.

1.   Hideo Kojima (programming influence and systems-minded auteur)

*   While primarily known as designer-director, Kojima’s hands-on approach to scripting, engine decisions, and cinematic tech (Metal Gear series) drove ambitious systems combining stealth AI, scripted events, and complex state machines.
*   Pushed integration of narrative-driven engines, motion capture pipelines, and cinematic tools into mainstream games.
*   Importance: influenced how game programmers integrate narrative, AI, and cinematic systems at high technical ambition.

Notes on selection and omissions

*   This list emphasizes programmers (or programmer-designers) whose code, engines, or system architectures changed how games are made. It includes hardware-software pioneers, engine authors, and influential indie developers.
*   Many other essential figures—Al Alcorn, Gary Gygax’s analog-to-digital lineage, Alexey Pajitnov (Tetris), Sid Meier (programmer-designer; simulation AI), Tim Sweeney (Unreal Engine), Amy Hennig (narrative systems), John Romero (design/programming at id), Brenda Laurel, and numerous unsung engine architects—are also profoundly influential. Different criteria (pure technical breakthroughs, cultural impact, commercial success, or breadth of influence) would yield different top-ten lists.
*   For time-sensitive or more exhaustive rankings, focus areas can be narrowed: engine authors, AI pioneers, graphics programmers, or indie innovators to highlight specialists.

Define "great programmer". If you're thinking of someone who can create an amazing game experience pretty much single-handedly, yes, I'd second Sid Meier, and add Brian Reynolds, who made an amazing Civ 2 prototype when he was working remotely in England (long before the days of distributed workforces); keep in mind, however, that Sid and Brian both self-identify as designers even though they have programming skills.

But for someone who defines "great programmer" as a person who loves solving really tough technical challenges, especially around performance, rendering, and modern consoles, I'd nominate Phil Teschner, and throw in Sam Lantiga at Valve.

If a great programmer is a visionary who helps create new technology that becomes an industry standard, Alex St. John should be on the list for his work on DirectX (which was the foundation for the Xbox).

If a great programmer is able to impart her knowledge to others and make the team better, it's a different list entirely. If a great programmer creates an amazing experience based on the capabilities of the platform, I'm sure there are many people who broke ground in early social and mobile games and created revolutionary experiences. If a great programmer makes an existing engine do things its creators never dreamed of, I'm sure Epic has some suggestions.

Great programmers also have a very different role today in game development than they did 20 years ago. Because game development has changed so much, you can specialize to an incredible degree; specialization in, say, graphics or AI doesn't make you greater (or less great) than your counterparts 20 years ago. Also keep in mind that because the industry is much larger than it was 20 years ago, there are many incredible programmers who don't get the PR love because they're working on a 200- or 300-person team; that doesn't mean they're less talented, just that the industry has changed significantly and programmers are often the unsung heros who help make the vision of the producers and designers a reality.

I think most of the answers here have good nominees, so I won’t repeat the most popular ones (Bill Budge, Ken Silverman, Jon Freeman and Anne Westfall, etc.), but I’d like to nominate a programmer who is often overlooked, but what he achieved was astounding.

This guy developed a game with a complete windowing GUI on an Apple II. It didn’t predate Pinball Construction Set, but what it did was much more complex. Whenever you clicked on a game element (say, a ship engine), a new window would pop up, populated with everything pertinent to that item. You could drag and drop within that window, and then dismiss it when you were done with it. Sound familiar?

And this paradigm worked for the whole game, not just some parts. Where many other games of the era made you type in a command (e.g. Wizardry for spells), this game employed icons.

This game was released about the same time as the first Macintosh, so it’s unlikely that the game tried to “copy” the Mac interface; there simply wasn’t enough time. The programmer said his GUI was inspired directly from the developments at Xerox PARC (the same place Apple took their inspiration for the Mac).

![Image 23](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-1b11349275d8f0ae5533834def0c8fda-lq)

While the gameplay, setting and objectives were engaging, that asn’t the point. This game employed an entire GUI that wouldn’t be commonplace for another 11 years, all in 64K of memory!

And that isn’t all. The game, if left unattended, would execute a self-running demo for the game’s planned sequel!

The programmer was Bruce Webster and the game was SunDog: Frozen Legacy. Why many probably haven’t heard of him is because after this game, he suffered from game programming burn out and quit the industry. He went on to write articles for BYTE magazine and to teach, also becoming CTO of a software company at one point. Now he’s teaching senior-level programming classes at his alma mater, BYU.

Webster developed the Apple II version of the game. About a year later, FTL released an Atari ST version of the game. He said one of his proudest moments was upon meeting one of the developers of the Atari ST version of the game. He said they were able to left entire sections of his code and re-use them verbatim because he used a Berkley-compliant Pascal compiler for the Apple II version, and they used a Berkley-compliant Pascal compiler for the Atari ST version as well. A great deal of the Atari ST version of the game is actually Webster’s code, though he never actively participated in its development.

Had he not suffered burn-out, the world may have been blessed with SunDog II: Old Scores to Settle and SunDog III: Blows Against the Empire. Too bad. If SunDog was anything to judge by, they would have been blasts.

# Ask the Developer Vol. 19: Donkey Kong Bananza — Part 1

*   This article has been translated from the original Japanese content. 
*   This interview was conducted before the game was released. 

In this 19th volume of Ask the Developer, an interview series in which developers convey in their own words Nintendo's thoughts about creating products and the unusual details they hone in on, we're talking to the developers behind the [_Donkey Kong Bananza_](https://www.nintendo.com/us/store/products/donkey-kong-bananza-switch-2/) game, a [Nintendo Switch™ 2](https://www.nintendo.com/us/gaming-systems/switch-2/features/) game that launches on Thursday, July 17.

* * *

## Check out the rest of the interview

*   [**Part 2: Voxel technology**](https://www.nintendo.com/us/whatsnew/ask-the-developer-vol-19-donkey-kong-bananza-part-2/) 
*   [**Part 3: Sparking interactions**](https://www.nintendo.com/us/whatsnew/ask-the-developer-vol-19-donkey-kong-bananza-part-3/) 

* * *

## **Part 1: Chain of destruction**

**First, can you introduce yourselves?**

**Kenta Motokura** (referred to as Motokura from this point on): Hello, I’m Kenta Motokura, the producer for _Donkey Kong Bananza_. Until now, I've mostly been involved in the development of 3D Mario (1) games, having directed _Super Mario 3D World_ (2) and _Super Mario Odyssey_ (3). In terms of Donkey Kong games, I worked on the character designs for _Donkey Kong Jungle Beat_ (4). As the producer for _Donkey Kong Bananza_, I crafted the game's concept and set the direction for the overall structure and player controls.

**(1)**_A term that refers to an action game in the Super Mario™ series in which Mario moves around in a 3D space. In contrast, 2D Mario games refer to side-scrolling 2D platformers in the same series._

**(2)**_A Wii U™ game released in November 2013. In this 3D platformer, up to four players can explore the Sprixie Kingdom, a land full of surprises, where new transformations, such as Cat Mario and Double Mario, were introduced. Additional accessories may be required for multiplayer mode, sold separately. Super Mario 3D World + Bowser's Fury, which includes additional modes, was released on Nintendo Switch in February 2021._

**(3)**_A Nintendo Switch™ game released in October 2017. In this 3D platformer, players join Mario and his hat-shaped ally Cappy on a globe-trotting adventure, exploring ancient ruins, big cities, and much more._

**(4)**_Released in 2005 on the Nintendo GameCube™ system in Europe and North America. A Wii™ version of the game was released in May 2009 in North America and June 2009 in Europe. As Donkey Kong, players explore various kingdoms in the jungle, the clouds, and the ocean with the help of powerful moves like punches and shockwaves. The Nintendo GameCube version is played with the DK Bongos accessory, while the Wii version is controlled with unique actions that utilize motion controls._

**Kazuya Takahashi** (referred to as Takahashi from this point on): Hello, I’m Kazuya Takahashi, one of the directors for this game. I joined Nintendo in 2020, but before that, I worked on a broad spectrum of games, including open-world RPGs and arcade games. For this game, I gave direction on the game design and worked on the level design, cut scenes, and text creation.

**Wataru Tanaka**(referred to as Tanaka from this point on): Hello, I’m Wataru Tanaka, another of the game's directors. I've been involved in the development of several 3D Mario games since _Super Mario Galaxy 2_. For _Super Mario Odyssey_, I implemented player controls and directed the core system of action elements. As the programming director for _Donkey Kong Bananza_, I mostly provided direction on the processing performance and utilization of system functions for Nintendo Switch 2, as well as enemy behavior.

**Daisuke Watanabe** (referred to as Watanabe from this point on): Hello, I’m Daisuke Watanabe, the art director. I was in charge of character design in the _Super Mario Galaxy_ series and joined _Super Mario 3D World_ as the design lead. I oversaw _Donkey Kong Bananza_'s overall art direction.

**Naoto Kubo**(referred to as Kubo from this point on): Hi, I’m Naoto Kubo, the sound director. I’ve previously composed music for _Super Mario Maker_ and led the overall sound development for _Super Mario Odyssey._ As the sound director for _Donkey Kong Bananza_, I coordinated overall sound development and controlled quality. I also composed some of the game's music myself.

**Thank you. It sounds like staff members who've previously worked on 3D Mario games, in particular****_Super Mario Odyssey_****, were central to****_Donkey Kong Bananza_****'s development. But how is it that the 3D Mario development team ended up creating a new game in the Donkey Kong series?**

**Motokura:** Development began when Koizumi-san (5) approached our team and said, “With an eye to expanding the Donkey Kong franchise further, I'd like the team that's been working on 3D Mario games to create a 3D Donkey Kong game.” The Donkey Kong series started with an arcade game created by Miyamoto-san (6). It featured a lot of things that were innovative for arcade games at the time, such as narrative-based gameplay and stage composition with varied design. Later on, we had success with the _Donkey Kong Country_ series (7) developed with Rare Ltd. (8), and I think those titles also represented a significant innovation as Super NES games with unique visuals. So this time around, tasked with developing a Donkey Kong game ourselves, we decided we were going to aim for another big innovation.

![Image 20](https://assets.nintendo.com/image/upload/f_auto/q_auto/dpr_1.5/c_scale,w_900/ncom/en_US/articles/2025/ask-the-developer-vol-19-donkey-kong-bananza/Part%201/Switch2_DKB_AskTheDevs_Inserted_01_EN_20250708)

We'd built up a lot of expertise in gameplay development for 3D action games through our work on 3D Mario games, including _Super Mario Odyssey_, but we needed to dive deeper into the fundamental question of “What is Donkey Kong?” So, our first step was to seek out Miyamoto-san and Koizumi-san.

**(5)** Yoshiaki Koizumi. Senior Executive Officer and Senior General Manager of the Entertainment Planning & Development Division. Served as the general producer for Nintendo Switch.

**(6)** Shigeru Miyamoto. Representative Director Fellow. _Super Mario_™, _Donkey Kong_™, _The Legend of Zelda_™, and _Pikmin_™ series creator.

**(7)** A game development company headquartered in the United Kingdom. In addition to the _Donkey Kong Country_ series, the company has also developed games such as _Banjo-Kazooie_ and _GoldenEye_ _007_ for the Nintendo 64™ system. It later became a development studio under Microsoft.

**(8)** A series of action games released for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System™ from November 1994 through November 1996 in North America. Players adventure through the jungle as the mighty Donkey Kong and his friends.

**And were you able to find out what Donkey Kong means to them?**

**Motokura:** Miyamoto-san, who was also involved in the development of the Donkey Kong games created by Rare Ltd. and Retro Studios, Inc. (9), put great emphasis on Donkey Kong's moves, such as Hand Slaps and blowing on things.

Hearing that made me realize the wide range of moves Donkey Kong has at his disposal, and that there’s potential to expand them even further. Koizumi-san, who was involved in both _Super Mario Odyssey_ and _Donkey Kong Jungle Beat_, highlighted Donkey Kong's massive arms as something that sets him apart from Mario. I felt that Koizumi-san put emphasis on Donkey Kong's strength, like delivering mighty punches or lifting heavy objects.

**(9)** A game development company located in Austin, Texas, United States. Founded in 1998, it has codeveloped games such as _Donkey Kong Country Returns_ and mainline games from the _Metroid Prime_ series.

![Image 23](https://assets.nintendo.com/image/upload/f_auto/q_auto/dpr_1.5/c_scale,w_900/ncom/en_US/articles/2025/ask-the-developer-vol-19-donkey-kong-bananza/Part%201/Inserted_02)

**I have the impression that the Donkey Kong series brings something new to the table with each installment. Where does this title fit in?**

**Motokura:** Well now... In a long-running series, novelty and continuity are both important, but we wanted this title to fully convey the appeal of Donkey Kong as a character. Meanwhile, we thought that by creating something new, leveraging our experience developing 3D Mario games, we'd have the opportunity to create two separate branches – 2D Donkey Kong and 3D Donkey Kong – just as we did with Mario games. So, keeping in mind that this game will come to symbolize 3D Donkey Kong, and with the theme of bringing Donkey Kong's strengths and new actions to the forefront, we thought the concept of “destruction” would be a good fit.

**So you aimed to develop a game that would leverage the unique aspects of Donkey Kong as a character. Speaking of which, Donkey Kong's character design has been given a makeover, right?**

**Watanabe:** That was a hot topic of discussion. People's impressions of Donkey Kong actually vary quite significantly from person to person. Donkey Kong began life in the arcades as Mario's nemesis, but since then he's had many guises depending on the game, be that a cool, rugged king of the jungle or a lovable goofball. So, rather than just giving him a simple design update, we strove for a design that would get to the core of what makes Donkey Kong who he is, bringing out his unique characteristics and appeal.

**Motokura:** We also interviewed people who'd drawn illustrations of Donkey Kong from way back to preserve the image of Donkey Kong in the mind of his creator, Miyamoto-san.

**Watanabe:** We got no shortage of advice. From general guidance regarding his body frame and unique facial expressions, right down to the smallest detail, like how his pointy hairdo is essential...but you can't make it too long. (Laughs)

![Image 24](https://assets.nintendo.com/image/upload/f_auto/q_auto/dpr_1.5/c_scale,w_900/ncom/en_US/articles/2025/ask-the-developer-vol-19-donkey-kong-bananza/Part%201/Inserted_03)

**Everyone:** (Laughs)

**Motokura:** Because the series has been played for such a long time, we pursued the “identity” of Donkey Kong himself in various aspects.

**Watanabe:** Also, as we were testing out various moves with a temporary character model in the early phases of development, it became apparent how much bigger Donkey Kong is than Mario, giving him a considerable on-screen presence. This meant we could properly showcase a wide range of facial expressions, and by combining them with powerful moves, we felt we could create something new in terms of game feel, too.

**Motokura:** When controlling a character in a 3D world, the player often sees them from behind, so we were also conscious of how Donkey Kong would look from the back while he's moving. The back view of Donkey Kong just looks like a mass of brown fur, which would make for a monotonous visual if we simply rendered him in 3D. That inspired us to make some creative adjustments to his outfit, such as giving him britches and suspenders. We also made his fur look rich and thick. Outside of this game, Donkey Kong has recently appeared in _The Super Mario Bros. Movie_ released in 2023 and in _Mario Kart World,_ but there's a basic character design which provided the foundation for those versions of Donkey Kong. That basic Donkey Kong design has been completely revamped. While overhauling the design, we returned to where it had all started. We took Miyamoto-san's original Donkey Kong as the basis, adding design elements from _Donkey Kong Bananza_ here and there.

![Image 25](https://assets.nintendo.com/image/upload/f_auto/q_auto/dpr_1.5/c_scale,w_900/ncom/en_US/articles/2025/ask-the-developer-vol-19-donkey-kong-bananza/Part%201/Switch2_DKB_AskTheDevs_Inserted_04_EN_20250708)

**Does that mean that all of the recent Donkey Kong designs, including those from the movie and****_Mario Kart World_****, have their roots in the original one created by Miyamoto-san, with elements of Donkey Kong from****_Donkey Kong Bananza_****added to it?**

**Motokura:** That's correct. _Donkey Kong Bananza_ sparked the creation of a design which I think better conveys the new Donkey Kong.

**His thick fur stands out compared to the previous design, making him look wilder. And yet, at first glance, his various facial expressions also give the impression that he's a comical and charming character. That said, I saw he can alter his appearance in this game by transforming.**

**Takahashi:** Smashing lots of terrain and collecting gold fills up the Bananergy gauge, allowing Donkey Kong to perform [Bananza transformations](https://www.youtube.com/live/YVUidGTR8xg?t=373s), in which he powers up by transforming into different animal forms. This idea emerged while we were searching for Donkey Kong's ability change. We were discussing how it might be fun if, once he transforms into a powerful Kong Bananza, he could deal out destruction in different ways, not just with regular punches, but with charge punches, piercing punches and the like. In Mario’s case, he progresses through the game by powering up and becoming bigger or using special abilities, but in this game, Donkey Kong can transform anywhere by harnessing the power of Bananza transformation. Being able to transform anywhere lets him chain together his destruction, which is the concept of this game. We thought that this chain of destruction would be compelling as an action game. And so it became one of the key gameplay elements we focused on in this title.

# Ask the Developer Vol. 19: Donkey Kong Bananza — Part 1

*   This article has been translated from the original Japanese content. 
*   This interview was conducted before the game was released. 

In this 19th volume of Ask the Developer, an interview series in which developers convey in their own words Nintendo's thoughts about creating products and the unusual details they hone in on, we're talking to the developers behind the [_Donkey Kong Bananza_](https://www.nintendo.com/us/store/products/donkey-kong-bananza-switch-2/) game, a [Nintendo Switch™ 2](https://www.nintendo.com/us/gaming-systems/switch-2/features/) game that launches on Thursday, July 17.

* * *

## Check out the rest of the interview

*   [**Part 2: Voxel technology**](https://www.nintendo.com/us/whatsnew/ask-the-developer-vol-19-donkey-kong-bananza-part-2/) 
*   [**Part 3: Sparking interactions**](https://www.nintendo.com/us/whatsnew/ask-the-developer-vol-19-donkey-kong-bananza-part-3/) 

* * *

## **Part 1: Chain of destruction**

**First, can you introduce yourselves?**

**Kenta Motokura** (referred to as Motokura from this point on): Hello, I’m Kenta Motokura, the producer for _Donkey Kong Bananza_. Until now, I've mostly been involved in the development of 3D Mario (1) games, having directed _Super Mario 3D World_ (2) and _Super Mario Odyssey_ (3). In terms of Donkey Kong games, I worked on the character designs for _Donkey Kong Jungle Beat_ (4). As the producer for _Donkey Kong Bananza_, I crafted the game's concept and set the direction for the overall structure and player controls.

**(1)**_A term that refers to an action game in the Super Mario™ series in which Mario moves around in a 3D space. In contrast, 2D Mario games refer to side-scrolling 2D platformers in the same series._

**(2)**_A Wii U™ game released in November 2013. In this 3D platformer, up to four players can explore the Sprixie Kingdom, a land full of surprises, where new transformations, such as Cat Mario and Double Mario, were introduced. Additional accessories may be required for multiplayer mode, sold separately. Super Mario 3D World + Bowser's Fury, which includes additional modes, was released on Nintendo Switch in February 2021._

**(3)**_A Nintendo Switch™ game released in October 2017. In this 3D platformer, players join Mario and his hat-shaped ally Cappy on a globe-trotting adventure, exploring ancient ruins, big cities, and much more._

**(4)**_Released in 2005 on the Nintendo GameCube™ system in Europe and North America. A Wii™ version of the game was released in May 2009 in North America and June 2009 in Europe. As Donkey Kong, players explore various kingdoms in the jungle, the clouds, and the ocean with the help of powerful moves like punches and shockwaves. The Nintendo GameCube version is played with the DK Bongos accessory, while the Wii version is controlled with unique actions that utilize motion controls._

**Kazuya Takahashi** (referred to as Takahashi from this point on): Hello, I’m Kazuya Takahashi, one of the directors for this game. I joined Nintendo in 2020, but before that, I worked on a broad spectrum of games, including open-world RPGs and arcade games. For this game, I gave direction on the game design and worked on the level design, cut scenes, and text creation.

**Wataru Tanaka**(referred to as Tanaka from this point on): Hello, I’m Wataru Tanaka, another of the game's directors. I've been involved in the development of several 3D Mario games since _Super Mario Galaxy 2_. For _Super Mario Odyssey_, I implemented player controls and directed the core system of action elements. As the programming director for _Donkey Kong Bananza_, I mostly provided direction on the processing performance and utilization of system functions for Nintendo Switch 2, as well as enemy behavior.

**Daisuke Watanabe** (referred to as Watanabe from this point on): Hello, I’m Daisuke Watanabe, the art director. I was in charge of character design in the _Super Mario Galaxy_ series and joined _Super Mario 3D World_ as the design lead. I oversaw _Donkey Kong Bananza_'s overall art direction.

**Naoto Kubo**(referred to as Kubo from this point on): Hi, I’m Naoto Kubo, the sound director. I’ve previously composed music for _Super Mario Maker_ and led the overall sound development for _Super Mario Odyssey._ As the sound director for _Donkey Kong Bananza_, I coordinated overall sound development and controlled quality. I also composed some of the game's music myself.

**Thank you. It sounds like staff members who've previously worked on 3D Mario games, in particular****_Super Mario Odyssey_****, were central to****_Donkey Kong Bananza_****'s development. But how is it that the 3D Mario development team ended up creating a new game in the Donkey Kong series?**

**Motokura:** Development began when Koizumi-san (5) approached our team and said, “With an eye to expanding the Donkey Kong franchise further, I'd like the team that's been working on 3D Mario games to create a 3D Donkey Kong game.” The Donkey Kong series started with an arcade game created by Miyamoto-san (6). It featured a lot of things that were innovative for arcade games at the time, such as narrative-based gameplay and stage composition with varied design. Later on, we had success with the _Donkey Kong Country_ series (7) developed with Rare Ltd. (8), and I think those titles also represented a significant innovation as Super NES games with unique visuals. So this time around, tasked with developing a Donkey Kong game ourselves, we decided we were going to aim for another big innovation.

![Image 20](https://assets.nintendo.com/image/upload/f_auto/q_auto/dpr_1.5/c_scale,w_900/ncom/en_US/articles/2025/ask-the-developer-vol-19-donkey-kong-bananza/Part%201/Switch2_DKB_AskTheDevs_Inserted_01_EN_20250708)

We'd built up a lot of expertise in gameplay development for 3D action games through our work on 3D Mario games, including _Super Mario Odyssey_, but we needed to dive deeper into the fundamental question of “What is Donkey Kong?” So, our first step was to seek out Miyamoto-san and Koizumi-san.

**(5)** Yoshiaki Koizumi. Senior Executive Officer and Senior General Manager of the Entertainment Planning & Development Division. Served as the general producer for Nintendo Switch.

**(6)** Shigeru Miyamoto. Representative Director Fellow. _Super Mario_™, _Donkey Kong_™, _The Legend of Zelda_™, and _Pikmin_™ series creator.

**(7)** A game development company headquartered in the United Kingdom. In addition to the _Donkey Kong Country_ series, the company has also developed games such as _Banjo-Kazooie_ and _GoldenEye_ _007_ for the Nintendo 64™ system. It later became a development studio under Microsoft.

**(8)** A series of action games released for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System™ from November 1994 through November 1996 in North America. Players adventure through the jungle as the mighty Donkey Kong and his friends.

**And were you able to find out what Donkey Kong means to them?**

**Motokura:** Miyamoto-san, who was also involved in the development of the Donkey Kong games created by Rare Ltd. and Retro Studios, Inc. (9), put great emphasis on Donkey Kong's moves, such as Hand Slaps and blowing on things.

Hearing that made me realize the wide range of moves Donkey Kong has at his disposal, and that there’s potential to expand them even further. Koizumi-san, who was involved in both _Super Mario Odyssey_ and _Donkey Kong Jungle Beat_, highlighted Donkey Kong's massive arms as something that sets him apart from Mario. I felt that Koizumi-san put emphasis on Donkey Kong's strength, like delivering mighty punches or lifting heavy objects.

**(9)** A game development company located in Austin, Texas, United States. Founded in 1998, it has codeveloped games such as _Donkey Kong Country Returns_ and mainline games from the _Metroid Prime_ series.

![Image 23](https://assets.nintendo.com/image/upload/f_auto/q_auto/dpr_1.5/c_scale,w_900/ncom/en_US/articles/2025/ask-the-developer-vol-19-donkey-kong-bananza/Part%201/Inserted_02)

**I have the impression that the Donkey Kong series brings something new to the table with each installment. Where does this title fit in?**

**Motokura:** Well now... In a long-running series, novelty and continuity are both important, but we wanted this title to fully convey the appeal of Donkey Kong as a character. Meanwhile, we thought that by creating something new, leveraging our experience developing 3D Mario games, we'd have the opportunity to create two separate branches – 2D Donkey Kong and 3D Donkey Kong – just as we did with Mario games. So, keeping in mind that this game will come to symbolize 3D Donkey Kong, and with the theme of bringing Donkey Kong's strengths and new actions to the forefront, we thought the concept of “destruction” would be a good fit.

**So you aimed to develop a game that would leverage the unique aspects of Donkey Kong as a character. Speaking of which, Donkey Kong's character design has been given a makeover, right?**

**Watanabe:** That was a hot topic of discussion. People's impressions of Donkey Kong actually vary quite significantly from person to person. Donkey Kong began life in the arcades as Mario's nemesis, but since then he's had many guises depending on the game, be that a cool, rugged king of the jungle or a lovable goofball. So, rather than just giving him a simple design update, we strove for a design that would get to the core of what makes Donkey Kong who he is, bringing out his unique characteristics and appeal.

**Motokura:** We also interviewed people who'd drawn illustrations of Donkey Kong from way back to preserve the image of Donkey Kong in the mind of his creator, Miyamoto-san.

**Watanabe:** We got no shortage of advice. From general guidance regarding his body frame and unique facial expressions, right down to the smallest detail, like how his pointy hairdo is essential...but you can't make it too long. (Laughs)

![Image 24](https://assets.nintendo.com/image/upload/f_auto/q_auto/dpr_1.5/c_scale,w_900/ncom/en_US/articles/2025/ask-the-developer-vol-19-donkey-kong-bananza/Part%201/Inserted_03)

**Everyone:** (Laughs)

**Motokura:** Because the series has been played for such a long time, we pursued the “identity” of Donkey Kong himself in various aspects.

**Watanabe:** Also, as we were testing out various moves with a temporary character model in the early phases of development, it became apparent how much bigger Donkey Kong is than Mario, giving him a considerable on-screen presence. This meant we could properly showcase a wide range of facial expressions, and by combining them with powerful moves, we felt we could create something new in terms of game feel, too.

**Motokura:** When controlling a character in a 3D world, the player often sees them from behind, so we were also conscious of how Donkey Kong would look from the back while he's moving. The back view of Donkey Kong just looks like a mass of brown fur, which would make for a monotonous visual if we simply rendered him in 3D. That inspired us to make some creative adjustments to his outfit, such as giving him britches and suspenders. We also made his fur look rich and thick. Outside of this game, Donkey Kong has recently appeared in _The Super Mario Bros. Movie_ released in 2023 and in _Mario Kart World,_ but there's a basic character design which provided the foundation for those versions of Donkey Kong. That basic Donkey Kong design has been completely revamped. While overhauling the design, we returned to where it had all started. We took Miyamoto-san's original Donkey Kong as the basis, adding design elements from _Donkey Kong Bananza_ here and there.

![Image 25](https://assets.nintendo.com/image/upload/f_auto/q_auto/dpr_1.5/c_scale,w_900/ncom/en_US/articles/2025/ask-the-developer-vol-19-donkey-kong-bananza/Part%201/Switch2_DKB_AskTheDevs_Inserted_04_EN_20250708)

**Does that mean that all of the recent Donkey Kong designs, including those from the movie and****_Mario Kart World_****, have their roots in the original one created by Miyamoto-san, with elements of Donkey Kong from****_Donkey Kong Bananza_****added to it?**

**Motokura:** That's correct. _Donkey Kong Bananza_ sparked the creation of a design which I think better conveys the new Donkey Kong.

**His thick fur stands out compared to the previous design, making him look wilder. And yet, at first glance, his various facial expressions also give the impression that he's a comical and charming character. That said, I saw he can alter his appearance in this game by transforming.**

**Takahashi:** Smashing lots of terrain and collecting gold fills up the Bananergy gauge, allowing Donkey Kong to perform [Bananza transformations](https://www.youtube.com/live/YVUidGTR8xg?t=373s), in which he powers up by transforming into different animal forms. This idea emerged while we were searching for Donkey Kong's ability change. We were discussing how it might be fun if, once he transforms into a powerful Kong Bananza, he could deal out destruction in different ways, not just with regular punches, but with charge punches, piercing punches and the like. In Mario’s case, he progresses through the game by powering up and becoming bigger or using special abilities, but in this game, Donkey Kong can transform anywhere by harnessing the power of Bananza transformation. Being able to transform anywhere lets him chain together his destruction, which is the concept of this game. We thought that this chain of destruction would be compelling as an action game. And so it became one of the key gameplay elements we focused on in this title.

# My Hardest Bug Ever

This is the story of the hardest thing I've ever debugged, from Crash Bandicoot 1.

[![Image 12: Picture of Dave Baggett](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt740a130ae3c5d529/bltcb2a877e00297bbe/650880056859a77a808b442b/Dave_Baggett.jpg?width=100&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale)](https://www.gamedeveloper.com/author/dave-baggett)

[Dave Baggett,](https://www.gamedeveloper.com/author/dave-baggett)Blogger
October 31, 2013

schedule 12 Min Read

![Image 13: Game Developer logo in a gray background | Game Developer](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt740a130ae3c5d529/blt2c2f608b8dadcd62/6a97e133db31b5be7767f1c7/GDE27_Placeholder_-_5.png?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale)

[](https://www.linkedin.com/sharing/share-offsite/?url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/programming/my-hardest-bug-ever)[](http://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/programming/my-hardest-bug-ever)[](http://www.twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/programming/my-hardest-bug-ever)[](https://www.reddit.com/submit?url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/programming/my-hardest-bug-ever&title=My%20Hardest%20Bug%20Ever)[](https://bsky.app/intent/compose?text=My%20Hardest%20Bug%20Ever%20-%20https%3A%2F%2Fwww.gamedeveloper.com%2Fprogramming%2Fmy-hardest-bug-ever)[](mailto:?subject=My%20Hardest%20Bug%20Ever&body=I%20thought%20the%20following%20from%20Game%20Developer%20might%20interest%20you.%0D%0A%0D%0A%20My%20Hardest%20Bug%20Ever%0D%0Ahttps%3A%2F%2Fwww.gamedeveloper.com%2Fprogramming%2Fmy-hardest-bug-ever)

(Originally posted on [Quora](https://www.quora.com/Programming-Interviews/Whats-the-hardest-bug-youve-debugged))

As a programmer, you learn to blame your code first, second, and third... and somewhere around 10,000th you blame the compiler. Well down the list after that, you blame the hardware.  
  
This is my hardware bug story.  
  
Among other things, I wrote the memory card (load/save) code for[Crash Bandicoot.](https://www.quora.com/Crash-Bandicoot-series)For a swaggering game coder, this is like a walk in the park; I expected it would take a few days. I ended up debugging that code for 6 weeks. I did other stuff during that time, but I kept coming back to this bug -- a few hours every few days. It was agonizing.  
  
The symptom was that you'd go to save your progress and it would access the memory card, and almost all the time, it worked normally... But every once in a while the write or read would time out... for no obvious reason. A short write would often corrupt the memory card. The player would go to save, and not only would we not save, we'd wipe their memory card.D'Oh.  
  
After a while, our producer at Sony, Connie Booth, began to panic. We obviously couldn't ship the game with that bug, and after six weeks I still had no clue what the problem was. Via Connie we put the word out to other PS1 devs -- had anybody seen anything like this? Nope. Absolutely nobody had any problems with the memory card system.  
  
About the only thing you can do when you run out of ideas debugging is divide and conquer: keep removing more and more of the errant program's code until you're left with something relatively small that still exhibits the problem. You keep carving parts away until the only stuff left is where the bug is.  
  
The challenge with this in the context of, say, a video game is that it's very hard to remove pieces. How do you still run the game if you remove the code that simulates gravity in the game? Or renders the characters?  
  
What you have to do is replace entire modules with stubs that pretend to do the real thing, but actually do something completely trivial that can't be buggy. You have to write new scaffolding code just to keep things working at all. It is a slow, painful process.  
  
Long story short: I did this. I kept removing more and more hunks of code until I ended up, pretty much, with nothing but the startup code -- just the code that set up the system to run the game, initialized the rendering hardware, etc. Of course, I couldn't put up the load/save menu at that point because I'd stubbed out all the graphics code. But I could pretend the user used the (invisible) load/save screen and asked to save, then write to the card.  
  
I ultimately ended up with a pretty small amount of code that exhibited the problem -- but still randomly! Most of the time, it would work, but every once in a while, it would fail. Almost all of the actual Crash code had been removed, but it still happened. This was really baffling: the code that remained wasn't really doing anything.  
  
At some moment -- it was probably 3am -- a thought entered my mind. Reading and writing (I/O) involves precise timing. Whether you're dealing with a hard drive, a compact flash card, a Bluetooth transmitter -- whatever -- the low-level code that reads and writes has to do so according to a clock.  
  
The clock lets the hardware device -- which isn't directly connected to the CPU -- stay in sync with the code the CPU is running. The clock determines the[Baud Rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baud)-- the rate at which data is sent from one side to the other. If the timing gets messed up, the hardware or the software -- or both -- get confused. This is really, really bad, and usually results in data corruption.  
  
What if something in our setup code was messing up the timing somehow? I looked again at the code in the test program for timing-related stuff, and noticed that we set the programmable timer on the PS1 to 1kHz (1000 ticks/second). This is relatively fast; it was running at something like 100Hz in its default state when the PS1 started up. Most games, therefore, would have this timer running at 100Hz.  
  
Andy, the lead (and only other) developer on the game, set the timer to 1kHz so that the motion calculations in Crash would be more accurate. Andy likes overkill, and if we were going to simulate gravity, we ought to do it as high-precision as possible!  
  
But what if increasing this timer somehow interfered with the overall timing of the program, and therefore with the clock used to set the baud rate for the memory card?  
  
I commented the timer code out. I couldn't make the error happen again. But this didn't mean it was fixed; the problem only happened randomly. What if I was just getting lucky?  
  
As more days went on, I kept playing with my test program. The bug never happened again. I went back to the full Crash code base, and modified the load/save code to reset the programmable timer to its default setting (100 Hz) before accessing the memory card, then put it back to 1kHz afterwards. We never saw the read/write problems again.  
  
But why?  
  
I returned repeatedly to the test program, trying to detect some pattern to the errors that occurred when the timer was set to 1kHz. Eventually, I noticed that the errors happened when someone was playing with the PS1 controller.Since I would rarely do this myself -- why would I play with the controller when testing the load/save code? -- I hadn't noticed it. But one day one of the artists was waiting for me to finish testing -- I'm sure I was cursing at the time -- and he was nervously fiddling with the controller. It failed. "Wait, what? Hey, do that again!"  
  
Once I had the insight that the two things were correlated, it was easy to reproduce: start writing to memory card, wiggle controller, corrupt memory card. Sure looked like a hardware bug to me.  
  
I went back to Connie and told her what I'd found. She relayed this to one of the hardware engineers who had designed the PS1. "Impossible," she was told. "This cannot be a hardware problem." I told her to ask if I could speak with him.  
  
He called me and, in his broken English and my (extremely) broken Japanese, we argued. I finally said, "just let me send you a 30-line test program that makes it happen when you wiggle the controller." He relented. This would be a waste of time, he assured me, and he was extremely busy with a new project, but he would oblige because we were a very important developer for Sony. I cleaned up my little test program and sent it over.  
  
The next evening (we were in LA and he was in Tokyo, so it was evening for me when he came in the next day) he called me and sheepishly apologized. It was a hardware problem.  
  
I've never been totally clear on what the exact problem was, but my impression from what I heard back from Sony HQ was that setting the programmable timer to a sufficiently high clock rate would interfere with things on the motherboard near the timer crystal. One of these things was the baud rate controller for the memory card, which also set the baud rate for the controllers. I'm not a hardware guy, so I'm pretty fuzzy on the details.  
  
But the gist of it was that crosstalk between individual parts on the motherboard, and the combination of sending data over both the controller port and the memory card port while running the timer at 1kHz would cause bits to get dropped... and the data lost... and the card corrupted.  
  
This is the only time in my entire programming life that I've debugged a problem caused by quantum mechanics.

# My Hardest Bug Ever

This is the story of the hardest thing I've ever debugged, from Crash Bandicoot 1.

[![Image 12: Picture of Dave Baggett](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt740a130ae3c5d529/bltcb2a877e00297bbe/650880056859a77a808b442b/Dave_Baggett.jpg?width=100&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale)](https://www.gamedeveloper.com/author/dave-baggett)

[Dave Baggett,](https://www.gamedeveloper.com/author/dave-baggett)Blogger
October 31, 2013

schedule 12 Min Read

![Image 13: Game Developer logo in a gray background | Game Developer](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt740a130ae3c5d529/blt2c2f608b8dadcd62/6a97e133db31b5be7767f1c7/GDE27_Placeholder_-_5.png?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale)

[](https://www.linkedin.com/sharing/share-offsite/?url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/programming/my-hardest-bug-ever)[](http://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/programming/my-hardest-bug-ever)[](http://www.twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/programming/my-hardest-bug-ever)[](https://www.reddit.com/submit?url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/programming/my-hardest-bug-ever&title=My%20Hardest%20Bug%20Ever)[](https://bsky.app/intent/compose?text=My%20Hardest%20Bug%20Ever%20-%20https%3A%2F%2Fwww.gamedeveloper.com%2Fprogramming%2Fmy-hardest-bug-ever)[](mailto:?subject=My%20Hardest%20Bug%20Ever&body=I%20thought%20the%20following%20from%20Game%20Developer%20might%20interest%20you.%0D%0A%0D%0A%20My%20Hardest%20Bug%20Ever%0D%0Ahttps%3A%2F%2Fwww.gamedeveloper.com%2Fprogramming%2Fmy-hardest-bug-ever)

(Originally posted on [Quora](https://www.quora.com/Programming-Interviews/Whats-the-hardest-bug-youve-debugged))

As a programmer, you learn to blame your code first, second, and third... and somewhere around 10,000th you blame the compiler. Well down the list after that, you blame the hardware.  
  
This is my hardware bug story.  
  
Among other things, I wrote the memory card (load/save) code for[Crash Bandicoot.](https://www.quora.com/Crash-Bandicoot-series)For a swaggering game coder, this is like a walk in the park; I expected it would take a few days. I ended up debugging that code for 6 weeks. I did other stuff during that time, but I kept coming back to this bug -- a few hours every few days. It was agonizing.  
  
The symptom was that you'd go to save your progress and it would access the memory card, and almost all the time, it worked normally... But every once in a while the write or read would time out... for no obvious reason. A short write would often corrupt the memory card. The player would go to save, and not only would we not save, we'd wipe their memory card.D'Oh.  
  
After a while, our producer at Sony, Connie Booth, began to panic. We obviously couldn't ship the game with that bug, and after six weeks I still had no clue what the problem was. Via Connie we put the word out to other PS1 devs -- had anybody seen anything like this? Nope. Absolutely nobody had any problems with the memory card system.  
  
About the only thing you can do when you run out of ideas debugging is divide and conquer: keep removing more and more of the errant program's code until you're left with something relatively small that still exhibits the problem. You keep carving parts away until the only stuff left is where the bug is.  
  
The challenge with this in the context of, say, a video game is that it's very hard to remove pieces. How do you still run the game if you remove the code that simulates gravity in the game? Or renders the characters?  
  
What you have to do is replace entire modules with stubs that pretend to do the real thing, but actually do something completely trivial that can't be buggy. You have to write new scaffolding code just to keep things working at all. It is a slow, painful process.  
  
Long story short: I did this. I kept removing more and more hunks of code until I ended up, pretty much, with nothing but the startup code -- just the code that set up the system to run the game, initialized the rendering hardware, etc. Of course, I couldn't put up the load/save menu at that point because I'd stubbed out all the graphics code. But I could pretend the user used the (invisible) load/save screen and asked to save, then write to the card.  
  
I ultimately ended up with a pretty small amount of code that exhibited the problem -- but still randomly! Most of the time, it would work, but every once in a while, it would fail. Almost all of the actual Crash code had been removed, but it still happened. This was really baffling: the code that remained wasn't really doing anything.  
  
At some moment -- it was probably 3am -- a thought entered my mind. Reading and writing (I/O) involves precise timing. Whether you're dealing with a hard drive, a compact flash card, a Bluetooth transmitter -- whatever -- the low-level code that reads and writes has to do so according to a clock.  
  
The clock lets the hardware device -- which isn't directly connected to the CPU -- stay in sync with the code the CPU is running. The clock determines the[Baud Rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baud)-- the rate at which data is sent from one side to the other. If the timing gets messed up, the hardware or the software -- or both -- get confused. This is really, really bad, and usually results in data corruption.  
  
What if something in our setup code was messing up the timing somehow? I looked again at the code in the test program for timing-related stuff, and noticed that we set the programmable timer on the PS1 to 1kHz (1000 ticks/second). This is relatively fast; it was running at something like 100Hz in its default state when the PS1 started up. Most games, therefore, would have this timer running at 100Hz.  
  
Andy, the lead (and only other) developer on the game, set the timer to 1kHz so that the motion calculations in Crash would be more accurate. Andy likes overkill, and if we were going to simulate gravity, we ought to do it as high-precision as possible!  
  
But what if increasing this timer somehow interfered with the overall timing of the program, and therefore with the clock used to set the baud rate for the memory card?  
  
I commented the timer code out. I couldn't make the error happen again. But this didn't mean it was fixed; the problem only happened randomly. What if I was just getting lucky?  
  
As more days went on, I kept playing with my test program. The bug never happened again. I went back to the full Crash code base, and modified the load/save code to reset the programmable timer to its default setting (100 Hz) before accessing the memory card, then put it back to 1kHz afterwards. We never saw the read/write problems again.  
  
But why?  
  
I returned repeatedly to the test program, trying to detect some pattern to the errors that occurred when the timer was set to 1kHz. Eventually, I noticed that the errors happened when someone was playing with the PS1 controller.Since I would rarely do this myself -- why would I play with the controller when testing the load/save code? -- I hadn't noticed it. But one day one of the artists was waiting for me to finish testing -- I'm sure I was cursing at the time -- and he was nervously fiddling with the controller. It failed. "Wait, what? Hey, do that again!"  
  
Once I had the insight that the two things were correlated, it was easy to reproduce: start writing to memory card, wiggle controller, corrupt memory card. Sure looked like a hardware bug to me.  
  
I went back to Connie and told her what I'd found. She relayed this to one of the hardware engineers who had designed the PS1. "Impossible," she was told. "This cannot be a hardware problem." I told her to ask if I could speak with him.  
  
He called me and, in his broken English and my (extremely) broken Japanese, we argued. I finally said, "just let me send you a 30-line test program that makes it happen when you wiggle the controller." He relented. This would be a waste of time, he assured me, and he was extremely busy with a new project, but he would oblige because we were a very important developer for Sony. I cleaned up my little test program and sent it over.  
  
The next evening (we were in LA and he was in Tokyo, so it was evening for me when he came in the next day) he called me and sheepishly apologized. It was a hardware problem.  
  
I've never been totally clear on what the exact problem was, but my impression from what I heard back from Sony HQ was that setting the programmable timer to a sufficiently high clock rate would interfere with things on the motherboard near the timer crystal. One of these things was the baud rate controller for the memory card, which also set the baud rate for the controllers. I'm not a hardware guy, so I'm pretty fuzzy on the details.  
  
But the gist of it was that crosstalk between individual parts on the motherboard, and the combination of sending data over both the controller port and the memory card port while running the timer at 1kHz would cause bits to get dropped... and the data lost... and the card corrupted.  
  
This is the only time in my entire programming life that I've debugged a problem caused by quantum mechanics.

**John D. Carmack II**[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carmack#cite_note-wired.com-2) (born August 21,[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carmack#cite_note-dob-1) 1970)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carmack#cite_note-wired.com-2) is an American [computer programmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_programmer "Computer programmer") and [video game developer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_developer "Video game developer"). He co-founded the video game company [id Software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Id_Software "Id Software") and was the lead programmer of its 1990s games _[Commander Keen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commander\_Keen "Commander Keen")_, _[Wolfenstein 3D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfenstein\_3D "Wolfenstein 3D")_, _[Doom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doom\_(1993\_video\_game) "Doom (1993 video game)")_, _[Quake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quake\_(video\_game) "Quake (video game)")_, and their sequels. Carmack made innovations in [3D computer graphics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3D_computer_graphics "3D computer graphics"), such as his Carmack's Reverse algorithm for [shadow volumes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_volume "Shadow volume").

In 2013, he resigned from id Software to work full-time at [Oculus VR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reality_Labs "Reality Labs") as their [CTO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_technology_officer "Chief technology officer"). In 2019, he reduced his role to Consulting CTO so he could allocate more time toward [artificial general intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_general_intelligence "Artificial general intelligence") (AGI).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carmack#cite_note-consultant-4) In 2022, he left Oculus to work on his AGI startup, Keen Technologies.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carmack#cite_note-:0-7)

## Biography

### Early life

Carmack was born in [Shawnee Mission, Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shawnee_Mission,_Kansas "Shawnee Mission, Kansas"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carmack#cite_note-wired.com-2) the son of local television news reporter Stan Carmack. He grew up in the [Kansas City metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City_metropolitan_area "Kansas City metropolitan area"), where he became interested in [computers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer "Computer") at an early age. He attended [Shawnee Mission East High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shawnee_Mission_East_High_School "Shawnee Mission East High School") in [Prairie Village, Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prairie_Village,_Kansas "Prairie Village, Kansas") and [Raytown South High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raytown_South_High_School "Raytown South High School") in nearby [Raytown, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raytown,_Missouri "Raytown, Missouri").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carmack#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKushner200320%E2%80%9322-8)

Carmack was introduced to video games with the 1978 [shoot 'em up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shoot_'em_up "Shoot 'em up") game _[Space Invaders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Invaders "Space Invaders")_ in the [arcades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arcade_game "Arcade game") during a [summer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer "Summer") vacation as a child. The 1980 [maze chase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maze_game "Maze game") arcade game _[Pac-Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pac-Man "Pac-Man")_ also left a strong impression on him. He cited [Nintendo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo "Nintendo") designer [Shigeru Miyamoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shigeru_Miyamoto "Shigeru Miyamoto") as the game developer he most admired.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carmack#cite_note-9)

As reported in David Kushner's _[Masters of Doom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masters\_of\_Doom "Masters of Doom")_, when Carmack was 14, he broke into a school with other children to steal [Apple II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II "Apple II") computers. To gain entry to the building, Carmack concocted a sticky substance of [thermite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermite "Thermite") mixed with [Vaseline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaseline "Vaseline") that melted through the windows. However, an overweight accomplice struggled to get through the hole and instead opened the window, setting off a silent alarm and alerting police. Carmack was arrested and sent for psychiatric evaluation. He was sentenced to a year in a juvenile home.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carmack#cite_note-slashdot-answers-10)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carmack#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKushner200321-11) He attended the [University of Missouri–Kansas City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Missouri%E2%80%93Kansas_City "University of Missouri–Kansas City") for two semesters before withdrawing to work as a freelance programmer.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carmack#cite_note-12)

### Career

[Softdisk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Softdisk "Softdisk"), a computer company in [Shreveport, Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shreveport,_Louisiana "Shreveport, Louisiana"), hired Carmack to work on _[Softdisk G-S](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Softdisk\_(disk\_magazine) "Softdisk (disk magazine)")_ (an [Apple II GS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_IIGS "Apple IIGS") publication), introducing him to [John Romero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Romero "John Romero") and other future key members of id Software such as [Adrian Carmack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrian_Carmack "Adrian Carmack") (no relation). Later, Softdisk would place this team in charge of a new, but short-lived, bi-monthly game subscription product called _Gamer's Edge_ for the IBM PC (DOS) platform. In 1990, while still at Softdisk, Carmack, Romero, and others created the first of the _[Commander Keen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commander\_Keen "Commander Keen")_ games, a series that was published by [Apogee Software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apogee_Software "Apogee Software"), under the [shareware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shareware "Shareware") distribution model, from 1991 onwards.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carmack#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKushner200363%E2%80%9366-13) Afterwards, Carmack left Softdisk to co-found [id Software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Id_Software "Id Software").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carmack#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKushner200374-14)

Carmack has pioneered or popularized the use of many techniques in computer graphics, including "[adaptive tile refresh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adaptive_tile_refresh "Adaptive tile refresh")" for _Commander Keen_,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carmack#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKushner200350-15)[ray casting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_casting "Ray casting") for _[Hovertank 3D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hovertank\_3D "Hovertank 3D")_, _[Catacomb 3-D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catacomb\_3-D "Catacomb 3-D")_, and _Wolfenstein 3D_, [binary space partitioning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_space_partitioning "Binary space partitioning") which _Doom_ became the first game to use,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carmack#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKushner2003142-16)[surface caching](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_caching "Surface caching") which he invented for _Quake_, [Carmack's Reverse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmack's_Reverse "Carmack's Reverse") (formally known as z-fail stencil shadows) which he devised for _Doom 3_, and [MegaTexture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MegaTexture "MegaTexture") technology, first used in _[Enemy Territory: Quake Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enemy\_Territory:\_Quake\_Wars "Enemy Territory: Quake Wars")_.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carmack#cite_note-17)_[Quake 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quake\_3 "Quake 3")_ popularized the [fast inverse square root](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fast_inverse_square_root "Fast inverse square root") algorithm.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carmack#cite_note-18)

Carmack's engines have also been licensed for use in other influential first-person shooters such as _[Half-Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half-Life\_(video\_game) "Half-Life (video game)")_, _[Call of Duty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Call\_of\_Duty\_(video\_game) "Call of Duty (video game)")_ and _[Medal of Honor: Allied Assault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal\_of\_Honor:\_Allied\_Assault "Medal of Honor: Allied Assault")_. In 2005, Carmack developed his first game for mobile phones, [Doom RPG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doom_RPG "Doom RPG").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carmack#cite_note-19)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carmack#cite_note-20)

On August 7, 2013, Carmack joined [Oculus VR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oculus_VR "Oculus VR") as their [CTO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_technology_officer "Chief technology officer").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carmack#cite_note-21) On November 22, 2013, he resigned from [id Software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Id_Software "Id Software") to work full-time at Oculus VR.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carmack#cite_note-polygon-3)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carmack#cite_note-22) Carmack's reason for leaving was that id's parent company [ZeniMax Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ZeniMax_Media "ZeniMax Media") did not want to support Oculus Rift.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carmack#cite_note-23) Carmack's role at both companies later became central to [a ZeniMax lawsuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ZeniMax_v._Oculus "ZeniMax v. Oculus") against Oculus' parent company, [Meta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meta_Platforms "Meta Platforms") (then known as Facebook), claiming that Oculus stole ZeniMax's virtual reality [intellectual property](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intellectual_property "Intellectual property").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carmack#cite_note-24)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carmack#cite_note-25)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carmack#cite_note-26) The trial jury absolved Carmack of liability, though Oculus and other corporate officers were held liable for trademark, copyright, and contract violations.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carmack#cite_note-27)
